content: 1. After extracting the juice, the sediment is allowed to settle at the bottom for removal, while the scum rises to the surface to be skimmed off. 2. During the cooling process, the liquid undergoes crystallization, often facilitated by stirring, resulting in the formation of sugar crystals. 3. Centrifuges are typically employed to separate the uncrystallized syrup from the sugar crystals. 4. The sugar produced can either be sold in its current form for use or subjected to further processing to create lighter grades of sugar. 5. This additional processing may occur in a different factory, potentially located in another country. 6. In the production of beet sugar, washed beets are sliced and their sugar content is extracted using hot water in a device known as a diffuser. 7. An alkaline solution, often referred to as milk of lime, combined with carbon dioxide from a lime kiln, is used to precipitate impurities in a process called carbonatation. 8. Following filtration, the juice is concentrated through evaporation to achieve a solid content of approximately 70%, and controlled crystallization is used to extract the sugar. 9. A centrifuge is then utilized to separate the sugar crystals from the liquid, which is recycled back into the crystallization stages. 10. When economic factors make further sugar extraction unfeasible, the remaining liquid, known as molasses, is discarded. 11. The resulting white sugar is sieved to produce various grades for commercial sale. 12. There is minimal perceptible difference between sugar derived from beets and that from sugarcane. 13. Specific tests can distinguish between beet and cane sugar, and some tests are designed to detect fraudulent misuse of EU subsidies or adulteration in fruit juices. 14. The production of sugar generates residues that vary significantly depending on the raw materials used and the location of production. 15. While cane molasses is often used in culinary applications, molasses from sugar beets is generally considered unpalatable for human consumption and is primarily used as feedstock for industrial fermentation or as animal feed. 16. Once dried, both types of molasses can serve as fuel for combustion. 17. So-called raw sugars, ranging from yellow to brown, are produced by clarifying the source syrup through boiling and drying with minimal chemical processing until it crystallizes into a solid. 18. Raw beet sugars are intermediate products in the processing of sugar-beet juice, en route to becoming white sugar. 19. Types of raw sugar include demerara, muscovado, and turbinado. 20. Countries like Mauritius and Malawi export significant quantities of specialty sugars. 21. Manufacturers sometimes produce raw sugar in the form of loaves rather than crystalline powder by mixing sugar and molasses, pouring the mixture into molds, and allowing it to dry. 22. This process results in sugar cakes or loaves, known as jaggery or gur in India, pingbian tang in China, and panela, panocha, piloncillo, or pão-de-açúcar in various parts of Latin America. 23. In South America, truly raw sugar, which is unheated and made directly from farm-grown sugarcane, has a limited market share. 24. Mill white sugar, also called plantation white, crystal sugar, or superior sugar, is raw sugar that retains colored impurities but is bleached white using sulfur dioxide. 25. Although common in sugarcane-growing regions, mill white sugar does not store or ship well, as its impurities can cause discoloration and clumping over time. 26. Blanco directo, a white sugar prevalent in India and other South Asian countries, is produced by precipitating impurities from cane juice using phosphatation, a process involving phosphoric acid and calcium hydroxide, similar to the carbonatation technique used in beet sugar refining. 27. In terms of sucrose purity, blanco directo is purer than mill white sugar but less pure than refined white sugar. 28. Refined white sugar has become the most common form of sugar in North America and Europe. 29. Refined sugar can be produced by dissolving raw sugar and purifying it through methods such as phosphoric acid treatment, carbonatation with calcium hydroxide and carbon dioxide, or various filtration techniques. 30. Further purification is achieved by filtering the sugar through activated carbon or bone char, depending on the location of processing. 31. Beet sugar refineries produce refined white sugar directly without an intermediate raw stage. 32. Refined white sugar is typically sold as granulated sugar, which is dried to prevent clumping. 33. Granulated sugar is available in various crystal sizes for home and industrial use, depending on the application. 34. Coarse-grained sugars, such as sanding sugar (also known as nibbed sugar or sugar nibs), are commonly used for decorating cookies, biscuits, and other desserts. 35. Normal granulated sugars, often used for table purposes, have a grain size of approximately 0.5 mm. 36. Finer grades of sugar are produced by selectively sieving granulated sugar. 37. Caster (or castor) sugar, with a grain size of about 0.35 mm, is commonly used in baking. 38. Superfine sugar, also known as baker's sugar, berry sugar, or bar sugar, is preferred for sweetening drinks or preparing meringues. 39. The finest grades include powdered sugar, 10X sugar, confectioner's sugar (0.060 mm), or icing sugar (0.024 mm), which are produced by grinding sugar into a fine powder. 40. Manufacturers may add a small amount of anti-caking agents, such as cornstarch (1% to 3%) or tricalcium phosphate, to prevent clumping. 41. Sugar cubes or lumps are also sold for convenient consumption of standardized amounts. 42. Sugar cubes are made by mixing sugar crystals with sugar syrup. 43. Jakub Kryštof Rad invented sugar cubes in 1841. 44. Brown sugars are produced during the later stages of sugar refining, either as fine crystals with significant molasses content or by coating white refined sugar with a cane molasses syrup. 45. The color and taste of brown sugars intensify with increasing molasses content, as do their moisture-retaining properties. 46. Brown sugars tend to harden when exposed to air, but proper handling can reverse this. 47. The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) define free sugars as all monosaccharides and disaccharides added to foods by manufacturers, cooks, or consumers, as well as sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, and fruit juices. 48. This definition includes all the sugars mentioned above. 49. The term free sugars distinguishes these forms from other culinary sugars added in their natural, unrefined state. 50. Natural sugars encompass all completely unrefined sugars, effectively excluding those defined as free sugars. 51. The WHO Technical Report Series 916 on Diet, Nutrition, and the Prevention of Chronic Diseases approves only natural sugars as carbohydrates for unrestricted consumption. 52. Natural sugars are found in fruits, grains, and vegetables in their natural or cooked forms. 53. Biochemists classify sugars as relatively simple carbohydrates. 54. Sugars include monosaccharides, disaccharides, trisaccharides, and oligosaccharides, which contain one, two, three, or more monosaccharide units, respectively. 55. Sugars contain either aldehyde groups (-CHO) or ketone groups (C=O), characterized by carbon-oxygen double bonds, which make them chemically reactive.
